Macedonia, though historically significant, was mostly under Persian control due to its mountainous terrain and poor conditions for agriculture. Sparta emerged as the dominant military power among the Greeks because of its flat landscape suitable for farming, which required a large slave workforce known as helots.

The primary concern for Spartans was maintaining control over these slaves, given their vastly larger numbers. Helots were both crucial resources and significant threats; thus, Spartans focused on turning boys into warriors from an early age. At six or seven, children were taken away to foster anxiety and aggression necessary for effective combat. They endured constant physical training and mentoring by older men until they reached 14 or 15 when initiations included nighttime missions where helots who broke curfew were killed.

The Romans, Aztecs, and Americans followed similar practices. Around the same period, Greece saw advancements in military tactics like hoplites, which formed tight phalanx formations to overpower enemies. Persians, meanwhile, developed horse archers but faced geographical constraints that prevented their use in mountainous regions or wider plains. Consequently, when Persia invaded Greece, it could not utilize its most effective weaponry, leading to the defeat of Persian forces at Marathon in 490 BCE.

This battle showcased Greek superiority in infantry warfare, setting the stage for ongoing conflicts between the two empires.
